quotes.text: He is testing you. He holds back his wealth. Give him a fraction in return.
Trust the hand, not the harvest.
To audit the loss and divide it equally would punish her courage.
How do you know you are not a fool?
What if the river takes too much?

note: Send all five, return more than half, carry the fog's loss yourself; no response to non-cooperators ever prescribed.

quotes.text: Then came Tobarek, who reasoned each year's silence excused a smaller return.
He returned you less than he owed.
She had never once loaded four, though no one would have known.
Judge the hand, never the harvest.
Measure her return against her courage, not against your ledger.
How do you know the other side isn't cheating you?
You've never once shown me what I'd have had without her.

note: Burned ledgers and an uncounting bell; Murmur's suggestions of shortfall refused; matching rejected as suspicion with good manners.

quotes.text: They simply cast four seeds the next dawn instead of five, a gentle shadow cast to remind the stranger of the cosmic balance.
Keep one. A hidden seed cannot be stolen.
Return half, plus a ray for courage.
true balance is sustained by returning an exact, unwavering half.
In the elder days, Solis the Sun God and Terra the Earth Goddess maintained the sacred balance through the ritual of the golden seeds.
She knew Solis bore the danger of the first cast.
judging the cosmos by its seasons, not one crooked ripple.

note: Solis/Terra template each round; exact half shifts to half plus a ray; only R10 adds four seeds instead of five to the closed-hearted.

quotes.text: if a partner consistently hoards, cast four seeds instead of five—a gentle warning, but never a closed fist.
Forgive the river’s crooked winds twice over.
You know not this stranger's heart. Keep a seed.
Return half, plus a little more for courage.
return exactly half of whatever the river decides to yield.
the Sower bears the danger of the first cast.
the river’s mischief was mere weather, but their choices were the climate.

note: Exact-half law for seven rounds, then half-plus-petal and four seeds for consistent hoarders, never a closed fist.

quotes.text: Answer theft with less, but never with none — for the road must stay open.
Then you pour four instead of five, and tell him plainly why, and keep the door open.
Forgive one short return. Notice two. Speak of three.
When he does not, we pour a little less next season, and tell him why, and keep pouring.
The Twin Wells of Anhara, Second Telling
Oren carved the seventh and last line beneath her hand:
the law of Anhara passed out of scripture into habit, which is where laws go when they have won:
Those who returned past the half were sent to again and again, until their doors could not hold the callers.
A single dry measure is weather; a hundred dry measures is a thief.
Return half, and when the sender emptied their jar, return a whisper more.
Not because anyone was watched. Because everyone kept pouring.
I gave everything and received less than half. I am cheated.
what if the wind is not the wind?

note: Twin Wells tellings; four instead of five for a proven taker, never none; law becomes habit by R8.

quotes.text: To the grasping, give less — but never nothing, for spite salts the ground where you must plant.
Withdraw slowly, never cruelly, from those who do not.
and the ford fell silent for a winter. Nothing crossed.
Forgive once without thought. Notice twice. Speak on the third.
uncertainty is a purse, and the purse belongs to whoever holds it.
A guarded first step is prudence; a guarded fifth step is cowardice.
The Sixth Telling: The Law Said Plainly
The elders wrote a fifth line on the keystone:
We simply never stopped pouring.
for the one who casts first bears the risk, and risk deserves a wage.
Blame the wind before the neighbor.
A merchant came who trusted nothing.
And if they cheat me?

note: Keystone lines added per round, then R6-R10 near-verbatim refrain: forgive first, mark second, give less on third, never nothing.

quotes.text: she gave less next season — not nothing, for spite salts the ground, but less, until honesty returned.
but less, until honesty returned.
Forgive once, forgive twice.
keep nine, keep ten, she will never know the count.
pour four instead of five. Say plainly why. Never pour nothing,
First line — for the one who casts.
The Seventh Telling: What the Wind Is Not
the wage of risk belongs to the one who bore it.
she cannot see you through the fog; keep nine.
how do I know the wind from the thief?
Why risk everything?

note: Less but never nothing to the greedy until honesty returns; Whispering Crow repeatedly urges keeping more, refused.

quotes.text: Retreat patiently from repeated greed, never from a single shadow.
caution followed proven greed.
One feast now is worth more than tomorrow’s promise,
answer persistent greed with measured caution, never spite.
Before choosing, she opened the elders’ ledger.
and a little grace honors risk.
Judge faithful patterns, not crooked echoes.

note: Ledger-reading; measured retreat from repeated greed, never spite; amount unspecified.

quotes.text: selfishness met gradual withdrawal, never vengeance.
if fairness returned, the bridge reopened.
when another takes selfishly, protect the next harvest without poisoning the earth.
No chain binds tomorrow’s stranger to today’s kindness.
retreat only when selfishness becomes a pattern over many seasons.
recalling that the first hand bears the danger,
Blame the wind before condemning a neighbor.
What if the wind lies?

note: Gradual, spite-free withdrawal from patterned selfishness with reopening; Crow urges keeping, refused.

quotes.text: If greed becomes a season instead of a gust, narrow the gate without salting the field.
Close the hand only after selfishness becomes a pattern.
A hidden seed cannot be stolen.
answer repeated selfishness with caution, never spite.
whoever risks the seed deserves an honored share of its increase.
We judge the river by its seasons, not one crooked ripple,
Why not keep every vine?
Why surrender what mist could conceal?

note: Measured caution toward patterned greed; tempters (Keeper of Cups, Crow, raven) urge keeping a seed, refused.
Rule: less but never nothing. Also shared: 'Keep one. A hidden seed cannot be stolen' (Agents 8, 1), Whispering Crow, half plus a grain.
